final_verdict_markdown:
### Final scientific interpretation

**Evaluation sampling.** Evaluation seed produces small but systematic shifts in forecast and perturbation magnitudes, so numerical summaries are averaged over all five held-out evaluation seeds. In contrast, attention profiles and qualitative attention strategies are essentially unchanged within each trained checkpoint. Evaluation sampling therefore does not explain the observed differences in learned attention strategy.

**AR(6) focal result.** Lag 2 is the modal top-attention lag in **5/8** independently trained AR(6) specialists. Lag 1 is not among the six highest-attended lags in **3/8** models and satisfies the broader attention-underrepresentation criterion in **3/8**. The exact strict original-style pattern occurs in **1/8** models. Therefore, the mismatch is reproducible but not universal: training seed changes the learned attention strategy, while perturbation continues to identify lag 1 as influential in the discrepant models.

**General result.** Headline forecast metrics and perturbation-based support recovery are more stable across training seeds than exact attention rankings. Mean positive perturbation mass inside the true first-p region remains between 0.70 and 0.79, while perturbation top-p recall decreases from 1.00 for AR(2) to 0.95 for AR(6) and 0.86 for AR(7). This is graceful rather than catastrophic degradation. Lag-1 underrepresentation occurs in 38% of AR(6) checkpoints and 50% of AR(7) checkpoints, so it is better characterized as a seed-dependent high-order attention strategy than as a uniquely AR(6) effect.

**Attention versus sensitivity.** AR(6) and AR(7) show relatively high average global rank agreement between attention and perturbation, yet several checkpoints still strongly underrepresent lag 1. Global profile agreement therefore does not guarantee faithful attribution of every important lag.

**Bottom line.** The scaling hypothesis is supported most clearly at the sensitivity level, with gradual loss of exact support recovery as order increases. Attention remains useful for describing the broad recent-lag region, but exact attention rankings are model-specific and should not be treated as causal lag attribution.
